facts.text: Lake Hart, a 1,881‑acre freshwater lake, gave the community its name but is a Class III impaired water body due to historic lead and mercury in fish.
The area was originally inhabited by the Timucua people, who occupied much of northern Florida before European contact in the 16th century.
After the war, Orange County evolved from cattle ranching introduced by Spanish colonists and expanded by “Cracker” cowboys who drove herds across open prairies.
Seasonal flooding keeps Lake Hart’s water level between about 55 and 64 feet, with a FEMA 100‑year flood elevation of 63 feet.
The lake’s vegetation index scores 47, indicating a healthy plant community dominated by native species, yet it still faces statewide mercury impairments in fish tissue.
Lake Hart sits at 28°23′16″N 81°13′45″W, roughly seven miles south of downtown Orlando, bordered by Boggy Creek to the east and the city limits to the north.
